content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is a significant health issue for premenopausal women. Medical treatments that avoid unnecessary surgical interventions are appealing, but there is considerable variability in clinical practice and uncertainty regarding the most effective therapy. Danazol, a synthetic steroid, exhibits anti-estrogenic and anti-progestogenic properties, along with weak androgenic effects. It works by suppressing estrogen and progesterone receptors in the endometrium, leading to endometrial atrophy (thinning of the uterine lining), reduced menstrual blood loss, and, in some cases, amenorrhea (absence of menstruation). The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of Danazol in managing heavy menstrual bleeding in women of reproductive age. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group's Specialised Register, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies up to April 2007. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing Danazol with placebo, other medical therapies, or different dosages of Danazol were included. Trials involving women with postmenopausal bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, or pathological causes of heavy menstrual bleeding were excluded. Nine RCTs involving 353 women met the inclusion criteria. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. The primary outcomes included menstrual blood loss (MBL), adverse effects, weight gain, withdrawals due to adverse effects, and dysmenorrhea. When data were unsuitable for meta-analysis, they were presented descriptively. The results showed that Danazol was more effective than placebo, progestogens, NSAIDs, and oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) in reducing menstrual blood loss, although the confidence intervals were wide. However, treatment with Danazol was associated with a higher incidence of adverse effects compared to NSAIDs (odds ratio [OR] 7.0; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.7 to 28.2) and progestogens (OR 4.05; 95% CI 1.6 to 10.2). Danazol significantly reduced the duration of menstruation compared to NSAIDs (weighted mean difference [WMD] -1.0 days; 95% CI -1.8 to -0.3) and a progesterone-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) (WMD -6.0 days; 95% CI -7.3 to -4.8). No randomized trials were identified comparing Danazol with tranexamic acid or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system. In conclusion, Danazol appears to be an effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding compared to other medical therapies. However, its use may be limited by its side effect profile, acceptability to patients, and the need for ongoing treatment. The small number of trials and their limited sample sizes restrict the strength of recommendations for clinical practice. Further studies are unlikely, and this review will not be updated unless new research becomes available.
